consumedBy.note: `module` is exactly a LearningModuleDefinition and nothing else. JSON.parse(file).module casts cleanly, and every key inside it — including each card's — is one the format declares. Everything this file adds for authoring lives outside `module`, so the player never sees a field it does not know.

module.title: Four Signatures, Then the Elm
module.subtitle: Three minutes. Everything a patrol can ask you is in here.

body: Boston, June 1774. Eight months the harbour has been shut. You run papers through this town for the Committee of Correspondence, and nobody looks at you twice.
Tonight you carry one sheet that matters. Read it before you carry it. Everything a patrol can ask you is in the next three minutes.

beats.text: Boston, June 1774. Eight months the harbour has been shut. You run papers through this town for the Committee of Correspondence, and nobody looks at you twice.
Tonight you carry one sheet that matters. Read it before you carry it. Everything a patrol can ask you is in the next three minutes.

body: Eight months ago a crowd put three cargoes of tea in that water.
Parliament's answer was to close the harbour. Not to fine the men who did it. To close the harbour.
Every hull in Boston is idle. Including everyone who never touched the tea.

beats.text: Eight months ago a crowd put three cargoes of tea in that water.
Parliament's answer was to close the harbour. Not to fine the men who did it. To close the harbour.
Every hull in Boston is idle. Including everyone who never touched the tea.

visuals.alt: Printed 1774 broadside headed 'BOSTON, May 12, 1774. Gentlemen,' set in period type, closing 'By Order of the Committee' over the signature of William Cooper, Town Clerk.
visuals.title: The Boston Committee of Correspondence on the Port Act, 12 May 1774
visuals.caption: A primary source: the Boston Committee of Correspondence's printed circular of 12 May 1774. It reports the act 'for blocking up the Harbour of Boston, with a Fleet of Ships of War,' and states the punishment reaches the whole town — the wharves 'ravished from the rightful Owners... to the utter Ruin of many worthy Citizens, in Revenge to the Patriotism of some, whom probably this Clause was inserted to punish.' Guilty and innocent, shut in together.
visuals.attribution: Boston Committee of Correspondence (signed William Cooper, Town Clerk). Library of Congress, Printed Ephemera Collection, digital id cph.3a50556 (LCCN 2006682758).

visuals.alt: 1774 mezzotint of Bostonians caged beneath the Liberty Tree, the cage labelled 'BOSTON', handed fish from a boat while British cannon and a fleet of warships surround them.
visuals.title: The Bostonians in Distress, 1774
visuals.caption: Period art: a 1774 London mezzotint of the closed port's toll — Boston caged under the Liberty Tree, ringed by cannon and warships, kept alive on relief passed up from a boat. Contemporary comment, not a documentary record.
visuals.attribution: Published London: R. Sayer & J. Bennett, 1774. Library of Congress, British Cartoon Prints Collection, digital id ppmsca.31272 (LCCN 2011647025).

check.prompt: The harbour is closed. Who does the closure fall on?
check.reinforcement: The Port Act closes the port itself, so it falls on every trade in Boston — the fishmonger who never touched the tea starves beside the men who did. That is what makes it the punishment of a whole town.

correctOption.text: Every trade in Boston, whoever was involved.
correctOption.feedback: The Act closes the port itself. The fishmonger who never touched the tea starves beside the men who did.

distractorPool.text: Only the men who destroyed the tea.
distractorPool.feedback: That would be a fine, or a trial. Parliament closed the whole harbour instead, which is what makes this the punishment of a town.

distractorPool.text: Only the merchants who dealt in tea.
distractorPool.feedback: Tea is not the boundary. The port is shut to all cargo.

distractorPool.text: Nobody yet; it is only a threat.
distractorPool.feedback: It took effect. The wharves are still.

distractorPool.text: Only the smugglers the customs house was already chasing.
distractorPool.feedback: No. The Act shuts the port to honest and dishonest cargo alike; it does not sort the town into guilty and innocent.

distractorPool.text: Only the Committee men who called the meeting.
distractorPool.feedback: No. It reaches the whole waterfront, not the organisers, which is exactly what makes it collective punishment.

body: Four acts, not one. The harbour shut. The colony's charter rewritten. Soldiers quartered. Trials moved out of reach.
Note what is not in them. Walking a street with paper in your hand is still lawful. That will matter tonight.

beats.text: Four acts, not one. The harbour shut. The colony's charter rewritten. Soldiers quartered. Trials moved out of reach.
Note what is not in them. Walking a street with paper in your hand is still lawful. That will matter tonight.

visuals.alt: Engraved harbour view of Boston with British warships and lines of troops landing at the Long Wharf.
visuals.title: A View of Part of the Town of Boston, and the Landing of Troops, 1768
visuals.caption: A primary source: Paul Revere's engraving of British troops landing at Boston in 1768. Six years on, the Coercive Acts quarter soldiers like these in the town and move trials out of a Boston jury's reach. It shows the occupation rather than the acts themselves; the specifics are named here, not read from it.

check.prompt: Which of these is still lawful in Boston tonight?
check.reinforcement: The four Acts shut the port, ended the town meeting, quartered soldiers, and moved trials out of reach — but none of them forbids carrying printed paper through the streets. That is what makes your cover hold.

correctOption.text: Carrying printed paper through the streets.
correctOption.feedback: Nothing in the four Acts forbids it. That is what makes your cover hold.

distractorPool.text: Holding a town meeting.
distractorPool.feedback: The Government Act ended them.

distractorPool.text: Landing cargo at the wharf.
distractorPool.feedback: The Port Act closed it.

distractorPool.text: Trying a soldier before a Boston jury.
distractorPool.feedback: The Administration of Justice Act moved those trials out of reach.

distractorPool.text: Choosing the colony's council by the town's own vote.
distractorPool.feedback: The Government Act rewrote the charter and put that choice in the Crown's hands.

distractorPool.text: Refusing to quarter a soldier the army sends to your parlour.
distractorPool.feedback: The Quartering Act is exactly what removed that refusal.

body: Boston elects its own assembly. It elects no member of Parliament.
The objection is not the cost. It is who laid it.

beats.text: Boston elects its own assembly. It elects no member of Parliament.
The objection is not the cost. It is who laid it. The town would say the same if the tax were a farthing, and it says the same about the men who wrote these Acts: Boston chose none of them.

visuals.alt: Printed page of the 1765 Stamp Act with the Act's title and opening clauses set in period type.
visuals.title: The Stamp Act, 1765
visuals.caption: A primary source, and from an earlier decade: the printed 1765 Stamp Act, where Boston first argued that a tax it never consented to could not bind it. That consent argument is the one carried forward to 1774 — and the date matters, because a 1765 document is not the Tea Party's punishment.

check.prompt: What is the objection to the tax?
check.reinforcement: Boston elects its own assembly but no member of Parliament, so the objection is who laid the tax — a body the town never chose — not what it costs.

correctOption.text: It was laid by a body Boston elects no one to.
correctOption.feedback: The objection is who laid it, not what it costs.

distractorPool.text: It costs too much.
distractorPool.feedback: They paid rates to their own assembly willingly. The amount was never the argument.

distractorPool.text: It was collected dishonestly.
distractorPool.feedback: The complaint is not corruption. It is authority.

distractorPool.text: It punished them for the tea.
distractorPool.feedback: Wrong decade. That is 1774; this argument is from 1765.

distractorPool.text: Parliament sits too far across the ocean to tax Boston well.
distractorPool.feedback: Distance is not the argument. Boston would reject a member it never chose even if he lived on Milk Street.

distractorPool.text: It should have been the King who laid it, not Parliament.
distractorPool.feedback: No. Boston chose the King's officers no more than Parliament. Consent turns on whether the town elected the body, and it elected neither.

body: They do not declare war. They cannot tax London.
What they can do is stop buying. Merchants sign not to import, and Britain's own merchants feel it and complain upward.

beats.text: They do not declare war. They cannot tax London.
What they can do is stop buying. Merchants sign not to import, and Britain's own merchants feel it and complain upward. A congress petitions and agrees the boycott; it does not raise an army.

visuals.alt: Printed 1774 broadside beginning 'WE the Subscribers, inhabitants of the town of [blank]', forty-nine lines of period type setting out a non-importation pledge and oath.
visuals.title: The Solemn League and Covenant, Boston, June 1774
visuals.caption: A primary source: the non-importation pledge the Boston Committee of Correspondence circulated in June 1774 — the very document the courier carries. Signers 'in the presence of God, solemnly... covenant and engage with each other' to 'suspend all commercial intercourse with the said island of Great Britain, until the said act for blocking up the said harbour be repealed.' Printed by Edes and Gill, Boston.
visuals.attribution: Boston Committee of Correspondence; printed by Edes and Gill, Boston, 1774. State Library of Massachusetts, Broadsides collection (via Digital Commonwealth).
visuals.rights: Public domain by age (imprint of 1774). The holding institution (State Library of Massachusetts, via Digital Commonwealth) records the item's rights status as 'not evaluated' and asserts no copyright.

check.reinforcement: They cannot declare war and cannot tax London, so they stop buying: merchants sign not to import, and Britain's own merchants feel it and complain upward. A congress petitions and agrees the boycott.

correctOption.text: They agree to stop importing British goods.
correctOption.feedback: Merchants sign not to import, and Britain's own merchants complain upward.

distractorPool.text: They declare war.
distractorPool.feedback: Not in 1774. A congress petitions and coordinates; it does not declare war.

distractorPool.text: They lay their own tax on British imports.
distractorPool.feedback: They have no power to tax London's goods. What they can do is refuse to buy them.

distractorPool.text: They petition the King and wait.
distractorPool.feedback: They do petition. But the pressure came from withholding trade.

distractorPool.text: They destroy another cargo, as they did the tea.
distractorPool.feedback: No. The answer this month is a signed pledge, not another night on the water — organised refusal, not more destruction.

distractorPool.text: They pay the duties quietly and hope the Acts are lifted.
distractorPool.feedback: No. The Covenant is the opposite of quiet compliance: a public agreement to stop the trade until the port reopens.

body: Mercer has printed one. It is worth nothing without names on it, and nothing again unless it is posted where the town can read it.
Four signatures, then the Liberty Elm. Patrols hold the streets. Stay off them.

beats.text: Mercer has printed one. It is worth nothing without names on it, and nothing again unless it is posted where the town can read it.

readingRateWpm.basis: Hasbrouck & Tindal (2017) oral reading fluency norms put the grade-8 spring 50th percentile at 151 words correct per minute. Silent reading of unfamiliar informational prose on a screen runs at or a little below that for this age, so 140 wpm is the planning rate and 120/160 bracket it. The windows are sized against 140 and, because the handler's lines are clipped rather than dense, carry generous slack for the acted beats and the checks.

excerptRateWpm.basis: Period statutory English at half the modern-prose rate. Retained for the format even though this deck carries no excerpt: the documents are shown as visuals (the Committee circular and the Covenant) rather than quoted as reading, per the design's clipped-line rule.

rescope.was: The 1765 Stamp-Act brief: identity, postwar revenue, stamp scope, representation, synthesis, insertion.
rescope.now: The 1774 Coercive-Acts case files: identity, the closure (file 1), what the law says (file 2), consent (file 3), the answer (file 4), the brief. Files 1 and 2 both teach INTOLERABLE_ACTS (collective punishment, then the scope and its legal boundary); file 3 teaches REPRESENTATION; file 4 teaches MERCANTILISM (non-importation).
rescope.narrationSource: The four case files' narration and the four check questions are the owner's verbatim script (docs/design brief, 2026-07-30). The brief card is a handoff, lightly adjusted from the same script (the em-dash in 'stay off them' was split into two sentences).
rescope.documents: File 1 -> the Boston Committee of Correspondence port-bill circular (primary; states the collective-punishment thesis nearly verbatim). File 4 -> the Solemn League and Covenant (primary; IS the non-importation object the courier carries). Files 2 and 3 carry SUPPORTING images only — Revere's Landing of Troops (occupation) and the 1765 Stamp Act (the earlier consent moment) — because no clean, rights-verified period PRIMARY document for the Acts' scope or for consent exists in content/m1/historical-sources.json; the presenter carries the specifics. The Able Doctor / bitter-draught cartoon is deliberately NOT used (bare-breasted allegory; grade-8 product). The Wolfe painting and the 1766 repeal satire are retired from the files. No provenance was fabricated.
